02 Executive Summary

A passive log became an active decision-support tool.

Enterprise operators rely on audit logs to investigate changes, troubleshoot issues, and maintain compliance across thousands of channels, VOD assets, households and device configurations. The existing experience forced operators to abandon their current task, open a disconnected module, and manually reconstruct what had changed, one field at a time.

I led the end-to-end redesign that embedded Version History directly inside the entity a user was already viewing, and introduced a side-by-side Version Comparison screen with semantic highlighting for Added, Updated, Removed and Unchanged values. That removes the disconnect between "where you are" and "what changed."

My Role

Research → IA → Flows → Wireframes → Visual Design → Prototype → Dev Handoff → QA

Timeline

4-6 weeks from discovery to developer handoff, run in weekly design critique cycles.

Team

2 Product Managers · 1 UI/UX Designer (me) · Backend Eng · Frontend Eng · QA

Tools

Figma · FigJam · Jira · Confluence · Developer pairing sessions

The short version

The Challenge

Audit history lived in a module completely disconnected from the entity it described, costing operators more time finding a record than understanding the change itself.

The Approach

Bring Version History into the entity's context, replace manual recall with recognition, and replace manual comparison with visual, color-coded differencing.

The Outcome

An 11-step investigation collapsed to 6 steps, with a reusable comparison pattern designed to scale across every entity type in the console.

03 The Problem

Finding the record took longer than understanding the change.

Audit Logs existed as a completely separate module. To investigate a single Channel, an operator had to leave it entirely, remember its Entity ID, rebuild a set of filters from memory, and search through a flat, chronological list, all before they'd even seen a single value that had changed.

1
2
3
4
01 · What the user sees

A flat, chronological table of every action across every service, with no relationship to the entity the operator was just working on.

02 · Problem

Filtering requires already knowing the Tenant ID, Entity ID and Entity Type. Recognition is replaced with recall, a core usability violation.

03 · Why this needed to change

Opening a record reveals metadata, but never how it differs from any other version. Comparison still happens entirely in the user's head.

04 · Expected outcome

Move history into the entity's context so operators recognize it, instead of searching a disconnected system for it.

1
Filter-first entry pointThe only way in is a filter panel. There is no contextual jump from an entity to its own history.
2
Bare Entity IDNumbers with no link back to the record, so users manually cross-reference the ID against the entity they came from.
3
Detail, not comparisonThe eye icon opens one static record, never a relationship between two points in time.
4
No entity groupingEvery service and entity type is interleaved in one list, adding noise to an already effortful search.

Before you can filter, you have to remember.

The filter drawer required a Tenant ID, Entity ID and Entity Type before returning a single result: three pieces of information the operator had to carry over from the page they'd just left.

Observation 1

Users were forced to remember information

Entity ID, Entity Type and Action Type all had to be memorized before search, a direct violation of recognition over recall.

Observation 2

Investigation required context switching

Leaving Channel Details to open the Audit module broke task continuity and forced users to hold context in their head.

Observation 3

Changes were compared manually

Even after opening a record, users had to open a second one and compare field-by-field, entirely from memory.

1
2

A detail drawer with nothing to compare against

The detail view surfaces rich metadata (user, session, entity, API context), but every field sits in isolation. There is no second version alongside it, so "what changed" is left entirely to the reader.

1
Timestamp, no baselineA single point in time is recorded, but nothing tells the reader what the value was immediately before it.
2
Repeated fields, no highlightEntity ID and Entity Type stack down the panel with identical visual weight, and nothing signals which of these actually changed.

What research kept surfacing

Finding 01

Operators investigate history while already viewing an entity. Nobody naturally starts from the Audit module.

Finding 02

Locating the correct audit record consumed more time than actually understanding the change itself.

Finding 03

Users wanted one clear answer to "What changed?" instead of "show me every record."

Finding 04

Comparing two versions side by side was the single most requested workflow, and it wasn't supported at all.

12 Design Exploration

Three ways to show history. Only one survives contact with real data.

Rejected

A · Horizontal Cards

Each version as a wide horizontal card in a scrollable row.

✕ Required excessive horizontal scrolling for entities with dozens of versions.

Rejected

B · Modal Window

History and comparison inside a single popup dialog.

✕ Became crowded almost immediately. No room to lay out a real comparison.

Rejected

C · Full Page Comparison

Dedicated standalone page for comparing any two versions.

✕ Broke the existing workflow. Users lost their place in the entity entirely.

Selected

D · Version History inside Entity Details

A dedicated Version History view launched from the entity, with Compare as its own focused step.

✓ Contextual · ✓ Scalable · ✓ Enterprise-friendly · ✓ No workflow interruption

Five decisions that shaped the final design

1 · Version History in Entity Details

Bring history to the user instead of making them search for it.

2 · Checkbox Selection

Select two versions directly from the timeline instead of typing Version IDs.

3 · Side-by-Side Comparison

Humans compare visually far faster than reading sequential records.

4 · Color Coding

AddedUpdatedRemovedUnchanged, identified at a glance.

5 · Metadata First

Show user, timestamp, version and entity before field-level detail, so users trust what they're comparing.

13 Final Solution · Screen 01

History becomes a button, not a destination.

Instead of adding another item to global navigation, Version History was placed exactly where an operator's eyes already land: the action bar of the entity they're viewing.

1
2
3
4
What the user sees

The same Channel Details page as before, with one new, unmissable action: Version History, sitting beside the existing Recordings action.

Problem it solves

Previously, history required remembering this Channel ID and leaving the page entirely. There was no visual cue that history even existed.

Why this solution

Contextual access beats global search. The system already knows which entity is open, so it should offer history instead of forcing the user to ask for it.

Expected outcome

Investigation starts in one click, from the exact place the user already is, preserving their mental model of the task.

1
Version History entry pointA first-class action, not buried in a menu. Placed where operators already look for entity-level tools.
2
Grouped with RecordingsSits alongside existing entity-level actions, reinforcing that history belongs to this record.
3
General Details in viewThe user never leaves the metadata they're actively verifying to check its history.
4
Channel ID stays visibleNo more memorizing an ID to search for elsewhere. It travels with the user automatically.
14 Final Solution · Screen 02

A timeline, not a table to search.

Version History lists every saved version in reverse-chronological order, because investigations almost always start with the most recent change, surfacing only what operators care about: version, timestamp, service, and who made the change.

1
2
3
4
5
Chronology

Most recent version at the top. Operators almost always investigate a recent change first, so recency should never require sorting or filtering to reach.

Metadata hierarchy

Primary: version & timestamp. Secondary: service & user. Supporting: action performed. Scannable in seconds, not minutes.

Version selection

Selection happens via checkbox, directly in the timeline: no dropdowns, no typing a Version ID from memory.

1
Compare Version, disabledDeliberately muted until a valid selection exists. Nothing to click into an error state.
2
Checkbox selectionConsidered dropdowns and manual Version ID entry first, but checkboxes on the timeline were fastest and least error-prone.
3
Reverse-chronological orderNewest version first, matching how operators naturally start an investigation.
4
Service & User columnsSecondary metadata that builds trust before a user commits to comparing two specific versions.
5
Progressive loading"Load More" keeps long-lived entities with hundreds of versions performant and scannable.
15 Final Solution · Screen 03

Error prevention, not error recovery.

The Compare button stays disabled until exactly two versions are checked. Rather than letting a user click Compare and then explaining why it failed, the interface removes the invalid action from the start.

1
1
2
Disabled → enabled CTA

Compare Version shifts from a light, low-contrast state to a solid, high-contrast purple the instant a second checkbox is ticked.

Error prevention in practice

Selecting 0, 1, or 3+ versions simply leaves the button inactive. There's no error message to write, read, or dismiss.

Why it matters

For a workflow run many times a day, removing even one dead-end click compounds into real time saved across a team.

1
Exactly two selectedThe comparison model only ever needs two points in time. The UI enforces that constraint visually, not with a validation message.
2
Compare Version, now enabledFull-contrast purple communicates "ready" at a glance, consistent with the product's semantic color language.
16 Final Solution · Screen 04 · The Centerpiece

From "read everything" to "see what changed."

This screen replaced manual, field-by-field inspection with a structured, color-coded comparison: the single biggest reduction in cognitive load across the whole redesign.

Added

New values introduced in the selected version.

Updated

Existing values that changed between versions.

Removed

Values that no longer exist in the newer version.

Unchanged

Fields that remain identical across both versions.

1
2
3
4
5
6
1
Metadata before detailTargeted vs. Source version, modified date, service and user, shown first so users trust exactly what they're comparing.
2
Keys legendA persistent legend defines Added, Updated, Removed and Unchanged once, so color never needs re-explaining per field.
3
Change Type filterUsers can isolate just what they came for, like "show me only what was Removed," instead of scanning everything.
4
Field-level diff, per languageChannel Name is compared across every locale simultaneously: strikethrough for removed, color for added or updated text.
5
Long-text comparisonDescriptions diff the same way as short fields, proving the pattern scales from a single word to a full paragraph.
6
Progressive disclosureDelivery, Security, Advertisement and Videos sections collapse by default, each tagged with its own change badge. Expand only what matters.

Why side-by-side, not inline or sequential

An inline change log stayed compact but made values hard to compare directly. A sequential view was simple to build but demanded constant scrolling. Side-by-side won on every dimension that mattered for enterprise accuracy: immediate visual comparison, faster scanning, and lower memory load.

Designing for the edge cases

No version history available, only one version existing, a failed comparison request, a deleted version, or restricted permissions: each state was defined explicitly so the interface never leaves an operator guessing what happened.

20 Developer Handoff

A design doesn't end in Figma. It ends in production.

What shipped with the handoff

  • Annotated Figma files with interaction detail
  • Component behavior for every UI state
  • Empty, loading and error state definitions
  • Version selection & comparison logic
  • API mapping for version data
  • Edge case documentation

Collaboration model

Weekly pairing sessions with Backend and Frontend engineers throughout implementation, plus hands-on Design QA to make sure the shipped experience matched intent, not just the static comps.

21 Lessons Learned

What this project reinforced.

The one that mattered most

Context matters

Users should complete a task without leaving their current workflow whenever possible. That single principle drove the entire redesign, every other decision in this doc traces back to it.

Visual > raw data

Presenting changes visually made technically dense audit data dramatically easier to interpret.

Enterprise UX is friction reduction

Removing one navigation step compounds meaningfully for users who repeat a task dozens of times a day.

Collaboration drives outcomes

Working closely with PM and Engineering throughout kept the solution both desirable and technically feasible.

22 Future Improvements

Where this pattern goes next.

23 Final Reflection
"This wasn't simply redesigning an interface. It was reimagining how enterprise users investigate change, turning Audit Logs from a passive record system into an active decision-support tool.

By embedding Version History within the user's existing context and replacing manual comparison with a structured, visual approach, the redesign reduced unnecessary effort while improving clarity and scalability, a pattern now ready to extend across every entity type in the console.
